lessons.title: 9. 气体、液体和固体的结构

nearbyText:
Where the dilute-gas approximation applies, intermolecular attraction is not enough to hold the molecules close together.
A gas has no fixed shape or volume and expands into the available space in its container.

This does not mean unlimited expansion under every condition;
a container and external pressure constrain its volume, and changes in temperature and pressure can also lead to condensation.
Repeated collisions of many molecules with the container walls produce gas pressure.

Liquids: Molecules in a liquid are close together (Figure $8$), so neighboring molecules constrain their motion, unlike motion in a dilute gas.
A simple approximation treats the neighbors as a temporary "cage," with a molecule vibrating near a local equilibrium position.

The cage is not fixed: its neighboring molecules are also moving.
Sometimes a rearrangement lets a molecule leave its old "cage" and enter another formed by new neighbors, a motion pictured as "hopping."

The source's statistical-mechanics estimate for water at room temperature gives an average residence time of one trillionth of a second and a time for one vibration of $10^{-12}\sim10^{-13}$ seconds.
These are order-of-magnitude estimates within this model, not fixed periods obeyed by all liquid molecules.

Under conditions where this approximation usually applies, increasing temperature shortens the average residence time.
The source attributes this picture of liquid motion to the Soviet physicist Yakov I. Frenkel;

its claim of priority is retained as historical attribution, not as an independently verified conclusion.
This approximate picture helps explain basic liquid properties qualitatively.

Yakov I. Frenkel ($1894\sim1952$) was a Soviet theoretical physicist who worked in several areas of physics.
The source credits him with creating modern liquid theory, laying foundations of ferromagnetic theory, and developing the first quantitative theory of uranium nuclear fission.

The source also describes his work on atmospheric electricity and the origin of Earth's magnetic field.
These statements preserve the textbook's historical attribution;
labels such as "creator" and "first" are not presented as independently verified, exclusive historical conclusions.
